fixtures.city_amends_note: The numbers are not amended, but they come from a different book and two rules differ. Philadelphia deletes Chapter 29 of the building code and takes the counts from Table 403.1 of the Philadelphia Plumbing Code, which the city does not amend (2021 International Plumbing Code table, the same rows as the state's Table 2902.1). The 50/50 split, rounding up and urinal substitution (Section 424.2) are unamended, so the state pack's worked examples stand. What Philadelphia changes: (1) a shared all-gender room is allowed only for occupancy classifications that need the same number of toilets and lavatories for men and women; (2) urinals are not permitted in a room designed for all genders; (3) partitions and doors around each toilet in an all-gender room must run from floor to ceiling.

amendment.text: All-gender multi-user toilet rooms: allowed where Table 403.1 requires the same number of toilets and lavatories for male and female; no urinals; partitions and doors enclosing each toilet extend from floor to ceiling; fixture count based on 100 percent of the occupant load. Single-user rooms are identified as available to all persons regardless of gender and count toward the required fixtures.
amendment.quote: P-403.1.1 Fixture calculations. To determine the occupant load of each gender, the total occupant load shall be divided in half. To determine the required number of fixtures, the fixture ratio or ratios for each fixture type shall be applied to the occupant load of each gender in accordance with Table 403.1. Fractional numbers resulting from applying the fixture ratios of Table 403.1 shall be rounded up to the next whole number. [...] Exceptions: [...] 2. Where multiple-user facilities are designed to serve all genders, the minimum fixture count shall be calculated 100 percent, based on total occupant load. In such multiple-user facilities, each fixture type shall be in accordance with ICC A117.1 [...] 3. Distribution of genders is not required where single-user water closets and bathing room fixtures are provided in accordance with Section 403.1.2. | P-403.1.2 Single-user toilet and bathing room fixtures. The plumbing fixtures located in single-user toilet and bathing rooms, including family or assisted- use toilet and bathing rooms that are required by Section 1109.2.1 of the International Building Code, shall contribute toward the total number of required plumbing fixtures for a building or tenant space. Single-user toilet and bathing rooms, and family or assisted-use toilet rooms and bathing rooms shall be identified as being available for use by all persons regardless of gender. | P-403.2 Separate facilities. Where plumbing fixtures are required, separate gender-based facilities shall be provided. Exceptions: * * * 5. Separate facilities shall not be required to be designated by gender where single-user toilet rooms are provided in accordance with Section 403.1.2. 6. For occupancy classifications requiring the same number of water closets and lavatories for male and female under Table 403.1, separate facilities shall not be required where rooms having both water closets and lavatory fixtures are designed for use by all genders and privacy for water closets is provided in accordance with Section 405.3.4. Urinals shall not be permitted in facilities designed for use by all genders. | 405.3.4 Water closet compartment. Each water closet utilized by the public or employees shall occupy a separate compartment with walls or partitions and a door enclosing the fixtures to ensure privacy. * * * P-405.3.4.1 Water closet compartments serving all genders. Partitions and doors enclosing a water closet in a toilet room serving all genders shall extend from floor to ceiling to ensure privacy and safety.
amendment.quote_note: Quoted from the certified copy of Bill No. 250645 with the struck-through model-code words left out. The PDF's text layer does not carry the strikethrough marks; the clean wording was checked against the certified copy of Bill No. 230653 (2023), which prints the same amendments in bold with no deletions, and against L&I's summary ('Omit reference to urinal. The 2023 amendments adopting provisions for all-gender facilities include a prohibition on urinals with these facilities'). In exception 2 of P-403.1.1 the 2026 bill's text layer also shows the model-code words 'and each urinal that is provided shall be located in a stall'; whether they are struck through cannot be told from the text layer, and exception 6 bans urinals in such rooms either way.

restrooms_city.rule: Two city rules add to the state's. (1) Section 9-636 of The Philadelphia Code (Bill No. 150668, signed October 20, 2015, in effect 90 days later): any entity that owns or leases a structure open to the general public, retail establishments and City-owned buildings included, must put gender-neutral signs on single-occupancy bathroom facilities for public use; it reaches existing rooms, not only new work. (2) The Philadelphia Plumbing Code: single-user toilet rooms are identified as available to all persons regardless of gender; a shared all-gender room is allowed where the table requires equal numbers for men and women, with floor-to-ceiling partitions and doors around each toilet and no urinals.
restrooms_city.quote: § 9-636. Gender-Neutral Bathroom Designation. (1) Definitions. [...] (b) Gender-neutral Signage. Signs identifying a facility without indicating a gender, such as “Restroom,” “Bathroom,” or “Toilet,” or symbols indicating the facility’s availability for use by any person, regardless of gender or gender identity. (c) Retail Establishment. A place of business open to the general public for the sale of goods or services. (2) Any entity that owns or leases a structure open to the general public, including but not limited to Retail Establishments and City-owned buildings, that currently has or at any time establishes one or more single-occupancy bathroom facilities for public use, shall provide Gender-neutral Signage for such facilities. [...] (3) Penalties. A violation of this Section shall constitute a Class III offense [...] SECTION 2. Effective Date. This Ordinance shall take effect 90 days after it becomes law. [Certification:] Passed by the City Council on October 8, 2015. The Bill was Signed by the Mayor on October 20, 2015. | 6. For occupancy classifications requiring the same number of water closets and lavatories for male and female under Table 403.1, separate facilities shall not be required where rooms having both water closets and lavatory fixtures are designed for use by all genders and privacy for water closets is provided in accordance with Section 405.3.4. Urinals shall not be permitted in facilities designed for use by all genders. | P-405.3.4.1 Water closet compartments serving all genders. Partitions and doors enclosing a water closet in a toilet room serving all genders shall extend from floor to ceiling to ensure privacy and safety.
restrooms_city.city_page_quote: People can use any bathroom consistent with their gender identity and any single occupancy bathroom in a retail establishment must have gender neutral signage. [...] The Gender Neutral Bathroom Law was passed in 2016 by City Council and is enforced by the City’s Department of Licenses and Inspections.
restrooms_city.note: The bill text was read in the certified copy; whether Section 9-636 has been amended since 2015 could not be checked in the code library. The city's web page gives 2016 as the year and describes the scope as retail establishments; the ordinance's wording is wider ('a structure open to the general public').

page.meta: Commercial bathroom partitions delivered to Philadelphia job sites. Price your restroom, pick a material and see Philadelphia's own restroom rules.
page.lead: Commercial bathroom partitions for Philadelphia offices, schools, universities and hospitals, shipped by freight to your job site.
page.stall_bullet: - **How many stalls:** Philadelphia's plumbing rules set the number of toilets by how many people use the building, with the same numbers as the rest of Pennsylvania. The table below shows what that means.
page.restroom_bullet: - **Single-user and all-gender restrooms:** a one-person restroom must be marked as open to everyone. A separate city law requires gender-neutral signs on single-occupancy restrooms in buildings open to the public, shops and City-owned buildings included, and it covers existing restrooms as well as new ones. Philadelphia allows a shared all-gender room where the required number of toilets is the same for men and women, and sets its own stall rule for it: the partitions and doors around every toilet must run from floor to ceiling, and urinals aren't allowed in the room. We found no Pennsylvania law that limits who may use which restroom.
page.permit_bullet: - **Permits:** Philadelphia requires a building permit for work that changes the interior of a building. Its list of work that needs none includes ordinary repairs, painting, cabinets, countertops and similar finishing work, and movable partitions no taller than 5 feet 9 inches. It doesn't name toilet partitions fixed to the floor or wall, so ask the Department of Licenses and Inspections (311, or 215-686-8686 from outside the city) whether your replacement needs one. Buildings on the city's historic register don't get these exemptions automatically. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.confirm_office: the Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I)
page.stalls_intro: Philadelphia takes its toilet counts from its own plumbing rules, and the numbers match the rest of Pennsylvania. They are based on a building's capacity: the most people it is designed to hold at one time, worked out from its floor area. Half are counted as men and half as women, and any fraction rounds up. Every toilet needs a stall. Urinals are optional: in each men's room they may take the place of up to half of the required toilets in an office, and up to two thirds in a restaurant or school, and each urinal needs a screen.
page.stalls_after: These are minimums for the whole building, and the men's figures show toilets only, before any are swapped for urinals. An office with 25 people or fewer, or any space with 15 or fewer, can use one shared restroom. A shared all-gender room is counted on everyone in the building instead of half. In Philadelphia it can't have urinals, so every fixture in it is a toilet behind floor-to-ceiling partitions and a full-height door. A separate Pennsylvania law asks for two women's toilets for every men's toilet or urinal in new or largely rebuilt public middle and high schools, arenas, stadiums and convention halls, so ask L&I whether it covers your project.
page.capacity: To find your building's capacity, the building rules count an office at one person per 150 square feet of floor, a restaurant dining room at one per 15 square feet and a classroom at one per 20. Your architect or L&I sets the final number.
page.install_rule: Philadelphia requires a City contractor license from the Department of Licenses and Inspections for any business doing construction, demolition or repair work that needs no specialized trade license, and work under a building permit on a commercial building must be done by a licensed Philadelphia contractor. Pennsylvania has no state license for commercial installers. Confirm what your project needs with L&I. You don't need a permit to buy partitions.
page.faq_install_extra: A business doing construction work in Philadelphia needs a City contractor license.
page.public_jobs_bullet: - **Public jobs:** on projects paid for in whole or in part with public money and costing more than $25,000, school district work included, Pennsylvania law requires at least the wage the state Department of Labor & Industry sets for each trade in the county; maintenance work is not covered. The state issues its rates project by project. On federally funded building work in Philadelphia County the carpenter rate is $57.72 an hour plus $30.39 in benefits. Philadelphia has its own wage rule for City construction contracts over $2,000: the City's schedule sets $57.72 an hour plus $30.89 in benefits for a carpenter.
page.sales_tax_bullet: - **Sales tax:** 8% in Philadelphia: 6% state and 2% city. A seller located outside Philadelphia isn't required to collect the 2% city part. Where it doesn't, the buyer owes that part to the state as use tax.
page.buyers_extra: - **Universities and hospitals:** phenolic or stainless steel for busy public restrooms, and full-height stalls where a shared all-gender room is planned.

- Toilet counts in Philadelphia: The Philadelphia Building Code, Section B-2901 (Chapter 29 replaced by a reference to the Philadelphia Plumbing Code), in [Bill No. 260394](https://files.amlegal.com/pdffiles/Philadelphia/260394.pdf); The Philadelphia Plumbing Code, Sections 403.1, P-403.1.1, P-403.1.2 and P-403.2, in [Bill No. 250645](https://files.amlegal.com/pdffiles/Philadelphia/250645.pdf). notes: To confirm by phone before launch: whether a like-for-like replacement of anchored toilet partitions in a commercial restroom needs a Philadelphia building permit (L&I, 311 or 215-686-8686).

Philadelphia's all-gender rule means standard partitions (open at floor and top) don't meet the city's rule for a shared all-gender room: floor-to-ceiling partitions and doors are needed there. Worth a product link once the catalogue has a full-height privacy line.

The movable-partition height differs between two official texts: 5 ft 9 in on L&I's EZ standard (citing Section A-301.2.1) and 'less than 6 ft.' on the phila.gov building permit page. The page uses 5 ft 9 in; read Section A-301.2.1 in the code library in a browser.

The Philadelphia Code on American Legal (codelibrary.amlegal.com) refuses automated access. The amendments were read in certified copies of the ordinances (files.amlegal.com); check Sections P-403, P-405.3.4.1, A-301.2.1, 9-636 and 17-107 once in the code library in a browser.

The certified copy of Bill No. 250645 (plumbing code) has no effective-date section; L&I's bulletin makes the 2021 editions mandatory for applications from July 1, 2026. Confirm the plumbing code's effective date with L&I.
Sales tax: the date the 2% city rate began was not found on an official page (the state regulation still lists the original 1% from October 1, 1991). The page gives no date.

Public jobs: the state's own carpenter rate for Philadelphia County is issued per project behind a search form (dliweb.pa.gov/prevwage), so the page shows the federal rate and the City's schedule. Act 101 of 2026 changes the state wage law from December 21, 2026: recheck then.

The City's wage schedule is reissued several times a year (the one used is dated October 21, 2026), and the copy of Section 17-107 on phila.gov dates from April 2019: recheck the $2,000 threshold and the carpenter rate before launch.
Public school projects: whether the School District of Philadelphia's work is reviewed by L&I or another body was not researched.
